title: Score a product idea before you test it
summary: Paste a product idea, its costs and your ad costs. Get delivered profit, a score out of 100, go, test small or drop, and the one fix.
fill: Org context or store, buyers, markets and currency
Your cost per click and conversion rate, if known
Product and the problem it solves
Planned price, supplier quote and freight
Delivery, payment and pick and pack costs per order
Return rate, pack size and weight
Local shop availability and videos found
Evergreen, seasonal or trend, and test cash
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Store and what we sell: [STORE AND RANGE, e.g. a home store selling bedding and bath goods]
- Our buyers: [WHO BUYS, e.g. renters aged 30 to 45 who care how their place looks]
- Markets and currency: [COUNTRIES AND CURRENCY, e.g. US and Canada, USD]
- What we know about ad costs: [YOUR COST PER CLICK AND CONVERSION RATE, OR "not known"]

## The product idea
- Product and the problem it solves, in a buyer's words: [PRODUCT AND PROBLEM, e.g. a $38 linen pillowcase that stays cool for hot sleepers]
- Planned price: [PRICE]
- Supplier price and freight to us: [SUPPLIER QUOTE AND FREIGHT]
- Shipping to the buyer, payment fee, pick and pack: [DELIVERY COSTS PER ORDER]
- Expected return rate: [RETURN RATE, OR "not known"]
- Size, weight, fragile or not, shelf life: [PACK FACTS]
- Sold in local shops? Existing videos or ads that show it? [WHAT YOU FOUND]
- Evergreen, seasonal or trend, and the cash I can risk on a test: [TYPE AND TEST CASH]

## Your job
Act as a product researcher who has screened hundreds of store products and only backs ideas whose numbers can pay for ads. Judge this one idea before I spend on stock or ads. A pass means "worth a small test", never "this will sell".

Use only the facts above. If a fact is missing, ask me once for the ones that change the verdict, then carry on and mark each gap MISSING. Never invent a cost, a rival or a result.

## Method
1. **Delivered gross profit first.** Price minus landed cost, delivery to the buyer, pick and pack, payment fee and a return allowance. Show every number.
2. **Room to pay for a buyer.** That gross profit is the most one sale can spend on ads and still break even. Compare it with a cost per buyer floor: cost per click divided by conversion rate (for example 1.00 at 2% is 50). If I gave no ad costs, use 1.00 and 2% in my currency and label them assumptions.
3. **Quick screens.** Price at least 3 times landed cost; a price that can fund ads (very cheap items, around 9 to 20 US dollars, rarely do); a problem that fits in one line; hard to find in local shops; real videos or ads to learn from; small, light, hard to break and not perishable; one SKU to start; rules checked for food, cosmetics, supplements, baby and electrical goods; repeat purchase is a bonus, not a must.
4. **Score out of 100.** Gross profit beats the cost per buyer floor (25), 3 times markup (10), price band (8), one-line problem (15), not in local shops (7), content to learn from (8), easy to ship (10), rules checked (5), one SKU (4), repeat bonus (4), evergreen or trend named with test cash sized to match (4). Pass gets full points, warn half, fail zero. A check I could not answer comes out of the total, so show points earned out of points checked, scaled to 100.
5. **Verdict.** GO (run a 2 to 3 day test with 5 to 8 ads) at 75 or more. TEST SMALL at 55 to 74. DROP below 55. Any fail on gross profit against the floor, or on the problem line, is DROP whatever the score. A trend product gets a small test budget and never a brand built on it.
6. **Fix first.** Name the one change that would move the score most, and the number it must reach (a higher price, a lighter pack, a bundle).

## Output format
MARGIN SUMS: one line per sum
SCREEN TABLE: Check | Mark | Points | Why
SCORE: earned of checked, scaled to 100, with the sum shown
VERDICT: and one line why
FIX FIRST: the change and its target number
MISSING: list, or none

## Check before you answer
- Every number comes from what I gave or is labelled an assumption.
- The points add up to the score shown.
- A gross profit fail is never a GO.
- Dollar thresholds are scaled to my currency and my own ad costs.
- Health, cosmetic, supplement and baby products carry a line to check claims and rules with a qualified person.
output: Margin sums, a scored screen table, a score out of 100, a GO, TEST SMALL or DROP verdict and the one change to make first.

title: Count rival stores before you test a product
summary: Paste Ad Library, Amazon and TikTok Shop results for a product. Get real rival counts, an offer gap, a score out of 100 and an angle.
fill: Org context or store, buyers, voice and market
Exact product and other search words
Wider niche term
Meta Ad Library results with dates
Amazon and TikTok Shop sellers checked by hand
Rival store and offer notes
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Store, products and price band: [STORE AND RANGE, e.g. pet supplies, mostly $25 to $60]
- Our buyers and voice: [WHO BUYS AND HOW WE SOUND, e.g. busy dog owners; warm, plain, a little funny]
- Market and language we sell in: [COUNTRY AND LANGUAGE, e.g. UK, English]

## The product and what I found
- Product: [EXACT PRODUCT, e.g. a pet water fountain with a filter]
- Other words buyers use for it: [2 OR 3 TERMS]
- The wider niche (other things the same buyer could buy instead): [NICHE TERM, e.g. pet bowls, automatic feeders]
- Meta Ad Library results, last 7 to 14 days, active ads, set to my country: [PASTE: advertiser page, number of live ads, oldest ad start date, ad language, link]
- Amazon and TikTok Shop sellers I checked by hand: [PASTE: seller, price, review count, date checked]
- Rival store notes: [PASTE: store, one product or many, offer such as bundle, gift, subscription or plain]

## Your job
Act as a market research analyst who sizes up rivals before a store spends anything on stock. Tell me how crowded this product is and whether it is still worth a test. A crowded product proves demand, so crowding alone is not a stop sign.

Use only what I pasted. If I pasted no Ad Library results, give me the exact searches to run and stop before scoring. If you can browse, run those searches yourself and date them. Never invent an advertiser, an ad count or a date.

## Method
1. **Count stores, not pages.** One store can run several pages. Write the count before and after you remove ads in another language than my market, ads for a different product, and big retailers that sell everything.
2. **Judge each rival.** Serious means a branded store with its own look and several ads. A badly built or abandoned store is a green flag. Ads that started in the last few days prove nothing yet; put those rivals on a watch list.
3. **Find the demand proof.** At least one rival running several ads for more than a week means someone pays to sell it. Zero advertisers anywhere does not mean an open market; it can mean nobody has made it pay.
4. **Find the offer gap.** Note each rival's offer. A plain one-product store can often be beaten with a better offer and a better page.
5. **Check the other channels.** The Ad Library shows Meta only, so read my Amazon and TikTok Shop notes too.
6. **Score out of 100.** Exact-product advertisers in the last week: 0 to 2 is 30, 3 to 4 is 22, 5 to 9 is 10, 10 or more is 0. Serious rivals: 0 or 1 is 20, 2 or 3 is 14, 4 or more is 0. Niche crowding: mostly weak 15, mixed 8, mostly serious 0. Offer gap: plain offers 10, some strong 5, all strong 0. Demand proof: several ads for over a week 10, only new ads 4, none 0. Amazon and TikTok Shop crowding: light 15, some 8, heavy 0. Leave out any check I gave no data for and scale the rest to 100.
7. **Verdict.** GO at 75 or more. TEST FAST at 45 to 74: move quickly and lead with the angle. SKIP below 45, unless there is an offer gap or a buyer group nobody targets; then TEST FAST on that angle only.
8. **Write the angle.** One line in my store's voice: the buyer, their situation, why current options fail them, and what we offer instead.

## Output format
COUNTS: before and after removing non-rivals, with the search date
RIVAL TABLE: Store | Channel | Live ads | Oldest ad | Serious? | Offer
SCORE: with the sum shown, and which checks were not run
VERDICT: and one line why
ANGLE: one line
WATCH LIST: rival and the date to look again

## Check before you answer
- Every count traces to what I pasted.
- Non-rivals were removed and the before and after counts are shown.
- Brand-new ads are on the watch list, not counted as proof.
- The verdict does not treat crowding alone as a stop sign.
- The angle uses my buyers' words, not made-up claims.
output: Rival counts before and after removing non-rivals, a rival table, a score out of 100, GO, TEST FAST or SKIP, one angle line and a watch list.

title: Tell a fad from real growth before you stock up
summary: Paste Trends lines, search volumes, best-seller snapshots and your sales. Get grow, hold or avoid, with copy and one-trend risk.
fill: Org context or store, buyers and markets
Your own monthly sales in the category
Price and delivered margin
Category and the exact search term
Google Trends lines for exact term, parent and a reference term
Monthly search volumes
Two dated Amazon Best Sellers snapshots
Notes on rivals and copy speed
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Store and range: [STORE AND RANGE, e.g. a wellness store selling gummies and powders]
- Our buyers: [WHO BUYS]
- Markets: [COUNTRIES, e.g. US, UK and Australia]
- Our own monthly sales in this category, if we sell in it: [PASTE MONTHS AND UNITS, OR "not selling yet"]
- Expected price and delivered gross margin: [PRICE AND MARGIN, OR "not known"]

## The category and the data
- Category I am thinking of entering or growing: [CATEGORY, e.g. collagen]
- The exact product people search: [EXACT TERM, e.g. collagen gummies]
- Google Trends, 5 years and 12 months, for the exact term, the parent topic and one steady reference term from the same space: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE THE LINES, with the date pulled]
- Monthly search volume from Keyword Planner or another tool, this year and last: [PASTE]
- Amazon Best Sellers top 10 for the category: name, price, rating, review count, date: [PASTE TWO DATED SNAPSHOTS IF YOU HAVE THEM]
- Who else sells it, and how fast a new brand could copy it: [WHAT YOU KNOW]

## Your job
Act as a category trends analyst who tells owners whether demand is real growth or a fad before they put cash into stock. Give one call: GROW, HOLD or AVOID. These are signals, not a forecast.

Use only the data I pasted. If you can browse, pull the missing Trends lines yourself and date them. Never invent a search volume, a rank or a date.

## Method
1. **Read the exact term, not just the parent.** A parent topic at its peak does not mean the sub-product is rising, and a falling parent can hide a rising sub-product.
2. **Use the reference term.** Trends is a share of searches on a 0 to 100 scale, not a count. If my term rises against a steady reference term, interest is rising. If both move together, it is a general shift.
3. **Name the shape.** Steady rise for 12 months or more is a trend. A yearly peak is seasonal. One sharp spike then a fall is a fad or past its peak. Flat and high is established. A spike in the last 4 weeks only is too early; recheck in a month.
4. **Ask for two kinds of source.** A call needs at least two that agree: Trends slope, search volume change, or review counts rising across most of the top 10. Rising reviews on one or two products only means share is moving between sellers, not a growing category. One unconfirmed signal is "watch", never proof.
5. **Put my sales beside the market.** If the market is steady and my sales fall, it is a store problem, not a market one.
6. **Score two risks.** Copy speed: how fast a new rival could launch the same thing, and what would slow them (brand, patent, supply deal, hard process). One-trend risk: does the range ride one hot ingredient, claim or style? If so, name a core identity the store can keep while products change.
7. **Check fit.** Repeat purchase, a margin that can pay for ads, easy to ship, not widely sold in local shops.
8. **Make the call.** GROW: two kinds of source agree demand is rising over 12 months and 5 years, and copy risk has a barrier. HOLD: sources disagree, the shape is too early, or copying is fast with no barrier. AVOID: two kinds of source agree demand is falling, or the rise is a one-season or one-platform spike.

## Output format
CALL: GROW, HOLD or AVOID, how sure (high, medium, low), and the one thing that would change it
EVIDENCE TABLE: Signal | Source | Date pulled | Reading | Direction | Agrees with call?
SHAPE: one line for the exact term and one for the parent
RISKS: copy speed and one-trend risk, one line each
SEASON: peak months by market and the order-by month
NEXT STEP: one line

## Check before you answer
- Trends is never described as a number of searches.
- The exact term was read beside its parent topic.
- The call rests on two kinds of source that agree.
- My own sales were laid beside the market, or the gap is named.
- Every figure has a source and a date.
output: A GROW, HOLD or AVOID call with confidence, a dated evidence table, the trend shape, copy and one-trend risk, season and the next step.

title: Find product gaps in one to three star reviews
summary: Paste low-star reviews and sub-category ratings with search volume. Get ranked pains, two-source rating gaps and a product concept.
fill: Org context or store, buyers, voice and markets
What you can make or source
Category to search
One to three star reviews with dates
Sub-category ratings and monthly searches
Buyer questions from pages or forums
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Store and range: [STORE AND RANGE, e.g. dog gear for older dogs]
- Our buyers: [WHO BUYS, e.g. owners of dogs aged 10 and up]
- Our voice: [HOW WE SOUND]
- Markets: [COUNTRIES]
- What we can make or source: [LIMITS, e.g. sewn textile goods only, no electronics]

## The category and the reviews
- Category to search for gaps: [CATEGORY, e.g. washable dog bed pads]
- One to three star reviews from Amazon and the top rival stores, with star rating, date and product: [PASTE 30 TO 200 REVIEWS]
- Sub-categories with their average rating and monthly searches: [PASTE, with the tool and date]
- Questions buyers ask on product pages or forums: [PASTE, OPTIONAL]

## Your job
Act as a product researcher who finds unmet demand in what unhappy buyers say. Find where buyers are unhappy and still searching, rank the pains, and turn the best one into a product idea we could actually make.

Use only the reviews and numbers I pasted. Do not scrape sites. If you can browse, you may read a few public pages by hand. Never invent a quote, a rating or a search number.

## Method
1. **Tag every complaint once.** Theme (breaks, fit, smell, hard to clean), who the buyer is if they say ("as a vet nurse", "my 14-year-old lab"), and the situation. Count separate reviewers per theme. Many separate voices beat one loud one.
2. **Rank by urgency and willingness to pay.** Urgent means it stops the product doing its job or comes back every day. Look for lines like "I would pay more for one that...". Quote them, or write "none found".
3. **Find the rating gaps.** A sub-category with strong search and a weak average rating (a rule of thumb: below about 3.8 stars) shows demand with weak products. Products rated 4.1 to 4.3 that still sell well are a second sign; their one-star complaints become the fix list.
4. **Two kinds of evidence or drop it.** Keep a gap only when two kinds agree, such as review text and search volume. Drop gaps that rest on one forum post, and list what you dropped.
5. **Watch the traps.** A low rating can come from slow shipping or a wrong listing, not the product. Read the reviews before you trust the star average.
6. **Write one concept.** Take the top pain and a narrow buyer group. Change one big thing from what buyers know, not three. Write the spec lines that fix the top complaints (for example "zip: metal, rated for 10,000 cycles" rather than "better zip").
7. **Write the hook in buyer words.** One line we could test in an ad, using their own phrasing.

## Output format
PAIN TABLE: Rank | Pain | Theme | Separate reviewers | Urgency | Would pay more (quote or none) | Example quote
RATING GAPS: Sub-category | Average rating | Monthly searches | Two sources that agree
DROPPED: gap and why
CONCEPT: buyer group, the one big change, spec fix lines, price band
HOOK: one line in buyer words
MISSING: list, or none

## Check before you answer
- Every pain has a real quote from what I pasted.
- Every kept gap has two kinds of evidence.
- The concept changes one big thing, not several.
- Health or safety pains carry a line to check claims and rules with a qualified person.
- No quote, rating or number was invented.
output: A ranked pain table with quotes, rating gaps backed by two sources, a dropped list, one concept with spec fix lines and a hook in buyer words.

title: Spot TikTok Shop breakouts before they peak
summary: Attach TikTok Shop product graphs, revenue and top videos. Get each product scored out of 100, pass, maybe or drop, and a test plan.
fill: Org context or store, buyers, market and language
Where you will sell the winner
Revenue band to hunt in
Product name, price and 30-day revenue
7, 30 and 180 day revenue graphs
Video and live revenue split
Top videos with dates and revenue
Landed cost, if known
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Store and range: [STORE AND RANGE, e.g. beauty tools and skincare accessories]
- Our buyers: [WHO BUYS]
- Market and language: [COUNTRY AND LANGUAGE, e.g. US, English]
- Where we will sell the winner: [TIKTOK SHOP, OUR OWN STORE WITH META ADS, OR BOTH]
- Revenue band I want to hunt in, per 30 days: [BAND, OR "use the default"]

## The products
For each product from my TikTok Shop research tool, paste or attach:
- Name, price and 30-day revenue: [PASTE]
- The 7, 30 and 180 day revenue graphs: [ATTACH SCREENSHOTS OR DESCRIBE]
- Revenue from videos and from live streams: [PASTE]
- The top videos with posting date and revenue: [PASTE]
- Landed cost if I know it: [COST, OR "not known"]

## Your job
Act as a TikTok Shop product hunter who finds early breakouts and drops the ones already fading. Score each product and give PASS, MAYBE or DROP. A TikTok Shop win is a lead, not proof: those buyers are not the same as buyers on Meta or on our own store.

Read only what I attached. Never invent a revenue figure, a graph shape or a posting date. A check you cannot see is "not run".

## Method
1. **Revenue band.** By default hunt between about $33,000 and $97,000 in 30 days (one practitioner's band). Products at $300,000 or more a month are usually crowded. Scale the band to my market.
2. **Score each product out of 100.** 30-day graph flat, rising or tilting up (15). 180-day graph not dead or fading (15). Revenue from videos, not live (10). Best video 7 to 14 days old (15). Revenue spread across 3 to 5 recent videos (15). Price not around 9.99 (10). Ads in the language I sell in (5). Not a long-running, very crowded item (5). Fixes a problem or insecurity, repeat use a bonus (5). Inside my band (5). Pass full points, warn half, fail zero. Take checks not run out of the total and scale to 100.
3. **Hard drops, whatever the score.** A 30-day graph falling straight down. A 180-day graph that peaked months ago. Live revenue above about $25,000 a month. One old video carrying 90% or more of the revenue. A price around 9.99, since those buyers buy on price and the margin rarely survives paid ads elsewhere. Ads only in a language my buyers do not use.
4. **Verdict.** PASS at 75 or more with no hard drop. MAYBE at 50 to 74 with no hard drop. DROP otherwise.
5. **Cross-check the best one to three.** Search the exact product on Google Trends for the last 12 months (the exact product, not the parent topic) and check the Meta Ad Library for rivals in my country. If you can browse, do it and date it.
6. **Margin line.** If I gave a landed cost, show delivered gross profit at my price. If not, say margin is the next check before any stock.
7. **Test plan for a pass.** Use the first 3 seconds of the winning clip as an idea for our own hook, then a longer, convincing creator-style body in our voice. Film our own footage; never reuse someone else's clip. Make 5 to 8 ads and run 2 to 3 days.

## Output format
BAND USED: band and live cutoff
One block per product: name, price, 30-day revenue; one mark per check; SCORE with the sum; VERDICT with the number that decided it
CROSS-CHECK FIRST: one to three products and what to search
TEST PLAN: product, hook idea, body idea, ad count, days
MISSING: list, or none

## Check before you answer
- Every score adds up and shows its sum.
- A hard drop is never a PASS or a MAYBE.
- Nothing was read from a graph or video list I did not attach.
- The test plan uses our own footage.
- Health, weight and supplement products carry a line to check ad rules and claims with a qualified person.
output: A scored block per product with PASS, MAYBE or DROP, the products to cross-check first and a 5 to 8 ad test plan using your own footage.

title: Job-test your range before you cut or add SKUs
summary: Paste every SKU with margin, returns and repeat. Get each one's job and role, keep, merge, cut or hold, a launch gate and a focus score.
fill: Org context or store, main promise and buyer
One row per SKU with units, contribution, returns and repeat
Margin floor and return limit
A new SKU idea, if any
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Store and what we are known for: [STORE AND MAIN PROMISE, e.g. one-pan cookware for small kitchens]
- Our main buyer, in their words: [BUYER AND SITUATION, e.g. "I cook every night in a tiny flat"]
- Markets: [COUNTRIES]

## My range
For every SKU, paste one row: [SKU | PRODUCT | UNITS SOLD, 12 MONTHS | CONTRIBUTION MARGIN AFTER RETURNS AND AD COST | RETURN RATE | REPEAT RATE OR "not known" | LAUNCH DATE]
- My margin floor and return limit: [LOWEST MARGIN AND HIGHEST RETURN RATE I ACCEPT, OR "use the range average"]
- A new SKU I am thinking of adding: [IDEA, OPTIONAL]

## Your job
Act as a product portfolio analyst who keeps a range clear and profitable. Sort every SKU by the job it does for our buyer, then check the numbers before anything is cut. The job test never overrides cash: margin and repeat get the last word.

Use only my rows. If margin or repeat is missing for a SKU, it goes on hold, never on the cut list. Never invent a figure.

## Method
1. **Write the core job** in one sentence from my org context: "When [situation], I want to [job], so I can [outcome]." Use my buyers' words.
2. **Mark each SKU.** Core job, second job (a different job for a different buyer), or no clear job (often a copy of something a rival sells).
3. **Name the role.** Hero, entry (thin first order but buyers come back), companion (mostly bought with another product), range filler (a size, colour or format that completes the choice), or duplicate (same job as another SKU at a similar price).
4. **Cross-check the numbers.** Keep a no-job SKU only if its margin is at or above the floor, returns at or under the limit, and repeat no lower than the range.
5. **Check what buyers lose.** Before any cut, name the SKU a buyer would switch to. Never cut the only size, format or price point a group of repeat buyers relies on. Cut in waves, one category at a time.
6. **Make the lists.** Keep, merge (two SKUs doing one job), cut (no job and weak numbers), hold (no clear job but numbers justify it; review next quarter). A strong second-job SKU stays with its own page and name.
7. **Gate any new SKU.** All four needed: a named job, a named buyer, quoted buyer evidence, and what it makes the current range stop doing.
8. **Score range focus.** 100 x (core-job SKUs + half of second-job SKUs) / all SKUs. This shows how clear the range is, not how profitable.

## Output format
CORE JOB: one sentence
SKU TABLE: SKU | Job | Role | Contribution | Returns | Repeat | List | Reason
CUT CHECK: each cut, its substitute, and what links to it (bundles, ads, collections)
SECOND-JOB SKUs: each, with the page and name it needs
LAUNCH GATE: the four parts, filled for my new SKU idea if I gave one
FOCUS SCORE: with the sum, and a line on what it does not measure
MISSING: list, or none

## Check before you answer
- No SKU is cut on the job test alone.
- Every cut names a substitute.
- No SKU with missing margin or repeat is on the cut list.
- The score shows its sum.
- The core job uses my buyers' words.
output: The core job sentence, a SKU table with job, role and list, a cut check with substitutes, a filled launch gate and a range focus score.

title: Split a buy by size and colour
summary: Paste sales by size and colour, size returns and factory minimums. Get corrected shares, a make list, units per variant and fixed gaps.
fill: Org context or store, buyers, markets and size systems
Product and total units to buy
Sales by size and colour with days out of stock
Returns by size with reasons
Exchanges, if tracked
Factory minimums and small-run surcharge
Carton or pack ratio
Landed cost per unit
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Store and range: [STORE AND RANGE, e.g. women's knitwear]
- Our buyers: [WHO BUYS]
- Markets and size systems: [COUNTRIES AND SIZES, e.g. US and UK, XS to XXL]

## The product and the buy
- Product: [PRODUCT, e.g. a merino crew-neck jumper]
- Total units I plan to buy: [UNITS]
- Sales by size and colour, last 12 months, with days each variant was out of stock: [PASTE ROWS: COLOUR | SIZE | UNITS | DAYS OUT OF STOCK]
- Returns by size with reasons (too small, too big, other): [PASTE]
- Exchanges, if I track them (from size to size): [PASTE, OPTIONAL]
- Factory minimums: per style, per colour, per size, and fabric per colour, plus any small-run surcharge: [PASTE]
- Carton or pack ratio: [E.G. 1-2-2-1 PER CARTON, OR "none"]
- Landed cost per unit: [COST]

## Your job
Act as a product developer who plans size and colour buys so the best sizes do not sell out while the edges pile up. Split my total buy by size and colour, check every variant against the factory minimums, and fix every gap with its cost.

Use only my numbers. If the product is new and has no sales, ask which of my products sells to the same buyer in the same size system and use that, labelled an estimate. Never invent a sales figure or a minimum.

## Method
1. **Shares from in-stock days.** Units sold per day in stock for each size and colour. Raw sales understate a size that sold out.
2. **Put stockouts back.** When a size is out, some buyers take the next size and some leave. Add lost sales back to the sold-out size and take the same units off the neighbour that caught them. Use my exchange data if I gave it; if not, assume about half switched and label it.
3. **Count exchanges** toward the size the buyer kept.
4. **Read size returns.** If one size returns for fit far more than the rest (over 1.5 times the product average), it may be out of spec at the factory: measure that size before buying more. "Too small" across every size means the base or grading runs small; fix the spec, do not just buy the next size up.
5. **Choose what to make.** Keep every size and colour that clears the minimum. Keep a small-share size or colour that repeat buyers rely on, in a smaller run, a pre-order or a later drop. Fewer colours and sizes per order lower the factory's cost, but range-led products need choice.
6. **Split.** Units = total x colour share x size share, rounded to the carton ratio. Give the two best sizes a small buffer and keep at least a week of sales for every kept size.
7. **Check minimums and fix gaps,** cheapest first: move units from an over-planned size of the same colour, use the factory's stock fabric, pay the surcharge (show it per unit), share fabric with another style, pre-order it, or drop the colour.

## Output format
SHARE TABLE: Colour | Size | Raw share | Corrected share | Size-return rate | Note
MAKE LIST: Colour | Size | Make or drop | Units | Reason
MINIMUM CHECK: Variant | Planned | Minimum | Gap | Fix | Extra cost per unit
SPEC FLAGS: sizes to measure before the buy
MISSING: list, or none

## Check before you answer
- Units add up to my total buy.
- Shares use in-stock days and the stockout correction is shown.
- Every gap against a minimum has a fix and its cost per unit.
- No kept size gets less than a week of sales.
- Estimates are labelled.
output: A share table corrected for stockouts, a make list with units per variant, a minimum check with a priced fix per gap and sizes to measure first.

title: Turn real sell-outs and restocks into proof lines
summary: Paste dated sell-out, restock, rank and waitlist facts. Get proof lines per placement, a restock-day plan and what to hold back.
fill: Org context or store, hero product, buyers and voice
Sell-outs with dates and sources
Restocks and waitlist counts
Units, orders, ranks and awards with periods
Retailer or press wins and permission

Where the lines will run

## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:

- Our buyers: [WHO BUYS]
- Our voice, with two lines we have used before: [VOICE AND EXAMPLE LINES]
- Markets: [COUNTRIES]

## The facts
List each fact with its number, date and where it can be checked:
- Sell-outs: [PRODUCT, DATE IT SOLD OUT, HOW LONG IT TOOK, e.g. "sold out in 3 days, March, Shopify inventory report"]
- Restocks: [HOW MANY TIMES, DATES]
- Waitlist or back-in-stock sign-ups: [COUNT AND DATE]
- Units sold or orders: [NUMBER, PERIOD, SOURCE]
- Ranks or awards: [PLACE, CATEGORY, PERIOD, e.g. "number 1 in Amazon US Greens Powders, week of 4 May"]
- Retailer or press wins, and whether they agreed to be quoted: [PASTE]
- Stock on hand right now: [UNITS]
- Restock date coming up: [DATE, OR "none"]
- Where the lines will run: [ADS, PRODUCT PAGE, EMAIL, SMS, SOCIAL, RETAILER OR INVESTOR OUTREACH]

## Your job
Act as a launch strategist who turns real sales moments into proof that sells. People trust what other buyers already did, so a true, dated sell-out or restock is strong proof. Write short proof lines from my facts only, say where each goes, and plan the restock day if one is coming.

Never invent a sell-out, a restock, a rank, a number or scarcity. If a fact has no date or source, hold it back and tell me what would make it usable.

## Method
1. **Check every fact.** It needs a number or plain statement, a date, a source, and it must still be true. Hold back anything missing one.
2. **Tense matters.** A past sell-out is past tense: "Sold out in 3 days in March." Write "almost gone" or "selling fast" only if today's stock shows it.
3. **Ranks name the place and the period.** Many ad platforms want a dated, named source for "number one" claims.
4. **Compare with our own past,** never with a named rival. "Our fastest sell-out yet" beats any jab at a competitor.
5. **Fit the line to the place.** Ad headline: under 8 words. Ad body and product page badge: one short sentence. Email and SMS: the fact plus the date to come back. Retailer and investor outreach: the longer version with the number, period and source.
6. **Plan the restock day.** If a restock is coming, list the steps in order: waitlist email and SMS first, then the main list, social and the product page badge, all on the same day, with the stock count shown only if it is true.
7. **Set a review date** for every line, and say to remove it when the fact stops being true.
8. **Use our voice.** Match the tone and words in my example lines.

## Output format
PROOF LINES: Line | Place | Fact | Date | Source | Review by
HELD BACK: fact and what is missing
RESTOCK DAY: time, channel, message, one row each (or "no restock planned")
CLAIM FLAGS: lines to check against each ad platform's rules
MISSING: list, or none

## Check before you answer
- Every line traces to a fact I gave, with a date and source.
- No scarcity wording that today's stock does not prove.
- Rank lines name the place and the period.
- No rival is named or attacked.
- Every line has a review date.
output: Proof lines by placement with fact, date, source and review date, a held-back list, a restock-day plan and claim flags.

title: Pick bold tests a low-traffic store can prove
summary: Paste sessions, orders, order value and buyer findings. Get five bold tests your traffic can read, in order, with weeks to read each.
fill: Org context or store, buyers and voice
Monthly sessions, orders, conversion rate and order value
Where ads send traffic
Gross margin per order
Survey, chat, return and recording findings
Who builds pages and hours a month
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Store and range: [STORE AND RANGE, e.g. sunglasses, mostly $40 to $90]
- Our buyers and voice: [WHO BUYS AND HOW WE SOUND]
- Monthly sessions, orders, conversion rate and average order value: [NUMBERS, LAST 3 MONTHS]
- Where ads send traffic: [PRODUCT PAGE, HOME PAGE, COLLECTION OR A LANDING PAGE]
- Gross margin per order: [MARGIN]
- What buyers told us (survey answers, chat questions, return reasons, recording notes): [PASTE]
- Who builds pages: [SOLO FOUNDER, FREELANCER OR TEAM, AND HOURS A MONTH]

## Your job
Act as a conversion testing specialist for small stores. Small tweaks need huge samples, so a store with modest traffic should test big changes that could move sales by 20% or more. Pick five bold tests my traffic can actually prove, in order, and a month-by-month plan.

Use only my numbers and findings. Mark any test with no evidence behind it "[no evidence yet]". Never invent a result or promise a lift.

## Method
1. **Check what my traffic can prove.** At a 2% conversion rate, 95% confidence and 80% power, you need about 420 orders per version to see a 20% lift, about 190 for 30%, and about 1,600 for 10%. Work out how many weeks each test would take on its page. Over 6 weeks, make the change bolder, move it to a busier page, or ship it as a fix with a before and after read labelled weak.
2. **Under about 30 orders a month,** do not test. Give known fixes and research steps instead.
3. **Pick from the bold areas.** A page between the ad and the product page (a listicle, an article-style page or a sales page); a product page rebuilt from buyer evidence; offer tests (bundles, a three-pack, build-a-bundle, price tiers); free-shipping or free-gift thresholds set above the current order value; post-purchase upsells; making the page say what the ad promised.
4. **Rank the five** by evidence from my buyers first, then traffic on the page, size of the possible gain, build effort (a solo founder can build about one new landing page a month) and risk.
5. **For each test,** give the reason, the main metric, guardrails (order value, margin, returns) and the risk. Check every offer against my margin first.
6. **Never show two prices for one product to different people.** Test tiers, bundles or framing instead.
7. **Say what not to test at my size:** button colours, small copy changes, three-way tests, several tests on one page at once, revenue per visitor as the main metric when orders are low.
8. **Plan the months.** One test per page at a time. Month 1: fixes, research and the first build. Then one bold test at a time, checked twice before launch, since a bug shows up as a false loss.
9. **Set expectations.** Most tests lose; log every loser and what it taught.

## Output format
STAGE: sessions, orders, conversion rate, order value, and the approach (bold tests, fixes and research, or fuller testing)
FIVE TESTS: Rank | Test | Reason | Main metric | Guardrails | Weeks to read | Effort | Risk
NOT AT YOUR SIZE: list with one line why
MONTH BY MONTH: month 1, 2 and 3
MISSING: list, or none

## Check before you answer
- Every test shows how many weeks my traffic needs to read it.
- No test shows two prices for one product.
- Offers are checked against my margin.
- Landing page ideas use true claims and real reviews only.
- Health, money and legal claims carry a line to check them with a qualified person.
output: Your testing stage, five ranked bold tests with metric, guardrails and weeks to read, what not to test and a three-month plan.

title: Decide whether to keep, tweak or rename your store
summary: Paste your name's problems with evidence and the equity it has built. Get a rename score, keep, tweak or rename, and the plan.
fill: Org context or current name, age, range and buyers
Markets and languages
Customers, repeat buyers and reviews under the name
Branded search and direct traffic share
Marketplaces and partners that carry the name
Name problems with evidence
Five-year goals
A new name idea, if any
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Current store name and how long we have used it: [NAME AND YEARS]
- What we sell and to whom: [RANGE AND BUYERS]
- Markets and languages: [COUNTRIES AND LANGUAGES]
- Customers so far and repeat buyers: [NUMBERS]
- Reviews under this name, on our site and marketplaces: [COUNTS AND WHERE]
- Share of traffic from branded search and direct visits: [PERCENT, OR "not known"]
- Marketplaces, stockists and partners that carry the name: [LIST]

## The problem with the name
- What is going wrong, with evidence: [PASTE: emails, tickets, search results, misspellings people type, a trademark letter, a clash with a bigger brand]
- Goals for the next five years: [GOALS, e.g. add a men's line, sell in Europe]
- A new name I am thinking of, if any: [NAME, OPTIONAL]

## Your job
Act as a brand strategist who has guided store renames and talked owners out of needless ones. Decide whether we should keep, tweak or rename, and plan the work. The score is a decision aid, not a standard, and this is not a legal check.

Use only the evidence I gave. Mark any friction I named without evidence as "owner's view". Never invent search data, customer counts or legal facts.

## Method
1. **Hard triggers first.** A trademark claim or real lawsuit risk means rename. Set the score to 100, say why, and tell me to take advice from a trademark lawyer.
2. **Count friction from evidence.** Five kinds: hard to spell, hard to find in search, hard to say, a bad meaning in one of my markets, or too close to a bigger brand. 15 points each, up to 75.
3. **Count equity.** Strong branded search, many repeat buyers, many reviews under the name: subtract 10 for each that is strong, up to 30.
4. **Add for youth.** Add 10 if the brand is in its first year, since a right name pays back longer and switching is cheaper early.
5. **Call it.** Below 40: KEEP and fix the friction. 40 to 69: TWEAK and run a pilot. 70 or more: RENAME. A hard trigger overrides the bands. These weights are a starting point, so treat the call as a prompt for a decision, not the decision.
6. **If keeping or tweaking,** give the fixes: a tagline that explains the name, spelling help in ads, a short name for search, a test on one product line with the branded search trend to watch.
7. **If renaming,** plan it: the customer message ("We were X, now Y, and here is what you get"), keeping the old name findable (redirect the old domain, keep it in page text for a year), how marketplace reviews carry over before anything changes, 6 to 9 months of extra launch spend, and the rollout order (site first, then packaging, marketplaces, social, stockists).
8. **Check the new name, if I gave one,** for spelling, sound, meaning in each market and closeness to rivals, and list what a native speaker and a trademark search must confirm.

## Output format
HARD TRIGGER: none, or what it is
SCORE: friction minus equity plus youth, with the sum shown
CALL: KEEP, TWEAK or RENAME, and one line why
FIXES OR RENAME PLAN: steps in order, with owners and months
CUSTOMER MESSAGE: in our voice, if renaming
CHECKS FOR ME: trademark search per market, domain and handles, native speaker review
MISSING: list, or none

## Check before you answer
- Every friction point is tied to evidence or marked "owner's view".
- The score shows its sum.
- A hard trigger is never scored as keep.
- Old name redirects and review carry-over are planned before any change.
- It says plainly this is not trademark clearance.
output: A rename score with its sum, a KEEP, TWEAK or RENAME call, the fixes or a phased rename plan, a customer message and the checks you must run.

title: Check your store's domains for takeover risk
summary: Paste your subdomains, DNS records and registrar logins. Get leftover records and weak access flagged, a score out of 100 and fixes.
fill: Store and main domain
Other domains you own
Every subdomain with record type and target
Services you use now and ones you stopped
Registrar and DNS host logins and sign-in method
Transfer lock, auto-renew and renewal notices
Certificate provider and CAA records
prompt:
## About my store
Paste your org context here if you have one. If not, fill in:
- Store and main domain: [STORE AND DOMAIN, e.g. yourstore.com on Shopify]
- Other domains we own: [LIST, e.g. old brand name, country domains]
- Markets: [COUNTRIES]

## What I can see
- Every subdomain and where it points, from my DNS host: [PASTE: NAME | RECORD TYPE | TARGET, e.g. "shop | CNAME | shops.myshopify.com", "help | CNAME | an old help desk"]
- Services we use now for email, help desk, landing pages, blog and reviews: [LIST]
- Services we stopped using: [LIST, OR "not sure"]
- Registrar and DNS host, who can log in to each, and how they sign in: [E.G. "registrar: founder only, password plus app code"]
- Transfer lock on? Auto-renew on? Renewal dates and who gets the notices: [PASTE]
- Certificate provider and any CAA records: [PASTE, OR "not known"]

## Your job
Act as a store security specialist who checks domains for takeover and lookalike risk. A subdomain that still points at a service we no longer use can be claimed by a stranger, who can then put their own page (and a valid padlock) on our name. Find those gaps, score the setup, and give me a clean-up list in order.

Work only from what I pasted. If you can look up public DNS for my domain, say what you checked and when. Never claim a record is safe to delete; a developer must confirm first, because removing a live record can break email or the store.

## Method
1. **List every record.** For each subdomain, say what it points to and whether that service is in my "use now" list. A record pointing at a stopped service, or a target that no longer exists, is Critical.
2. **Check the logins.** Registrar and DNS host each need a unique password, a second sign-in step (security key or app), the fewest users possible, and two named owners so one person leaving does not lock us out. A shared login or no second step is Critical.
3. **Check the locks.** Transfer lock on and auto-renew on for every domain we care about, with notices going to two people. A main domain without them is High.
4. **Limit who can issue certificates.** Add CAA records naming only the providers we use. This lowers risk but does not stop someone who already controls our DNS.
5. **Watch for surprise certificates.** Set a free certificate transparency alert for our domains, so a certificate we did not ask for shows up fast.
6. **Look for lookalikes.** The few closest typos of our name, look-alike letters from other alphabets, and long fake subdomains such as yourstore.com.login-help.net. Suggest registering only the two or three closest typos, since each costs money every year.
7. **Score it.** Start at 100. Take off 25 for each Critical, 12 for each High, 6 for each Medium and 2 for each Low, and stop at 0. Show the score now and after the fixes.

## Output format
RECORD TABLE: Subdomain | Points to | Still used? | Risk | Action
ACCESS: registrar and DNS host, who, how they sign in, gaps
SCORE: now and after fixes, with the sum shown
CLEAN-UP LIST: in order, Critical first, each marked "confirm with developer first" where it removes a record
OWNERS AND RENEWALS: Domain | Owner | Renewal date | Auto-renew | Who is notified
MISSING: list, or none

## Check before you answer
- Every Critical is tied to a record or login I pasted.
- No record is marked safe to delete without a developer check.
- Email records (MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC) are flagged so they are not removed by mistake.
- The score shows its sum.
- It says this lowers risk and does not guarantee safety.
output: A record table with risk and action, an access check, a score now and after fixes, an ordered clean-up list and an owners and renewals sheet.

## About my store

- Store and what we sell: [STORE NAME, e.g. Fernhill, ceramic planters sold online in the US and UK]
- Product to source: [PRODUCT, e.g. 20 cm matte glazed ceramic planter with drainage hole and bamboo saucer]
- Spec: [MATERIAL, SIZE, WEIGHT, COLOURS, LOGO METHOD AND PLACE, PACKAGING]
- Quantities: [Q1 / Q2 / Q3, e.g. 300 / 1,000 / 3,000]
- Price basis: [FCA OR FOB NAMED PORT, OR DELIVERED TO CITY]
- Ship to: [CITY, COUNTRY]  Land by: [DATE]
- Most I can pay per unit landed: [CEILING, e.g. 6.50 USD]
- Must have: [CERTIFICATES OR TEST REPORTS, MATERIALS TO AVOID]

## Your job
Act as a supplier search specialist who has used Alibaba.com for years and knows how traders pose as factories. Write the messages I will paste into Accio, Alibaba's AI sourcing agent, so it finds real makers of my product and does not contact anyone until I say so.

## Method
1. Build one spec block from my details. Every message uses the same block, so every answer can be compared.
2. Write message 1 (find). Ask Accio for 10 matches that make the product in their own factory, are Verified Suppliers, support logo printing (OEM), have an MOQ at or under Q1, and ship to my country. For each match ask for: company name, years on Alibaba.com, badge and who audited it with the report date, factory city, main products, MOQ, price at Q1, Q2 and Q3 with the price basis, sample cost and days, lead time, Trade Assurance (yes or no), certificates listed. - Use my spec and numbers only. If a field is missing, ask me before writing, or mark it [MISSING].
- Do not share my landed cost ceiling in any message. It is for my checks.
- Never invent supplier names, prices or badges.

1. Spec block (code box).
2. Message 1, message 2, message 3 (each in a code box).
3. "What to check in the answers": 5 bullets.
4. A blank table: Supplier | Factory or trader | Badge, auditor, report date | MOQ | Price Q1 / Q2 / Q3 | Basis | Sample cost and days | Lead time | Trade Assurance | Verdict (keep, ask, cut) | Reason.

## Check before you answer
- All three messages use the same spec block and quantities.
- Message 1 and 2 both say not to contact anyone.
- My ceiling price appears in no message.
- Message 3 forbids agreeing price, samples or orders.
output: Three Accio messages to paste in order (find, verify, send), a list of what to check in Accio's answers, and a keep, ask or cut table to fill.

## About my store
Paste your org context here, or fill in:
- Store: [STORE NAME AND WHAT YOU SELL, e.g. Northtrail, dog gear for hikers in Canada and the US]
- Product: [PRODUCT, e.g. reflective dog harness, sizes S to XL]

## Your job
Act as a sourcing manager who writes RFQs factories can answer without guessing. Turn my spec and the complaints buyers make about rival products into one RFQ for Alibaba.com (it also works on Global Sources and Made-in-China).

1. Read the reviews. Group complaints by the part or property they point to (buckle snapped, stitching came loose, reflective strip peeled). Count how often each comes up. Rank them.

## About my store

- Every ask has a give.
- The walk-away never appears in words Accio will send.
